title: Breaking Enigma
tagline: The mathematician who cracked the uncrackable code and saved millions of lives.

scenes.text: Bletchley Park, 1940. The German Enigma machine produces 158 quintillion possible settings. The Nazis change the settings every 24 hours. Every day, the Allied cryptanalysts must break the code fresh. Thousands of ships and lives depend on it.

scenes.speaker: Alan Turing
scenes.text: The human mind searches randomly. That won't work — there are too many possibilities. We need a machine that reasons systematically. A machine that can ask: what must be true, given what we know? A machine that thinks.

challenge.fact: The Enigma machine had 17,576 possible rotor starting positions (26×26×26). But with plugboard settings, the actual number of configurations was 158 quintillion — the Bombe exploited cribs (known plaintext) to narrow the search.
challenge.instruction: Before the Bombe, Turing practises on a simple shift. The hidden word is the crib Bletchley Park hunted for every morning — turn the wheel until it reads.

scenes.text: Turing's Bombe machine could test thousands of Enigma settings per minute, narrowing the search to a manageable number. Combined with cribs — known phrases the Germans always used — it broke Enigma reliably by 1941.

challenge.instruction: Five letters name the machine Turing designed to search Enigma's settings. Guess it before the day's key changes at midnight.
challenge.fact: Turing's Bombe ran through Enigma rotor settings at speed, rejecting every one that contradicted the crib, until only a handful were left for the codebreakers to test by hand.

scenes.speaker: Alan Turing
scenes.text: Can a machine think? Everyone says obviously not. But why not? Define thinking. If a machine can answer any question indistinguishably from a human, what exactly is missing? The question matters more than they know.

challenge.instruction: Every Enigma keypress closed an electrical path through the plugboard and rotors to a lamp. Complete the circuit so the signal gets through.
challenge.fact: Turing's Bombe was based on a Polish machine called the Bomba, which Turing and Gordon Welchman dramatically improved. At peak operation, 211 Bombe machines ran simultaneously at Bletchley Park.

scenes.text: After the war Turing went back to the idea he had published in 1936: a single universal machine that could carry out any computation written on its tape.

challenge.instruction: Back to the idea of 1936: a machine that reads a tape and rewrites it by rule. Wire the gates so the circuit gives the right output on every row.
challenge.fact: In 1946 Turing designed the Automatic Computing Engine (ACE) for the National Physical Laboratory, one of the first complete designs for a stored-program computer; a Pilot ACE ran in 1950.

challenge.instruction: Put the steps in order so the machine accepts the right strings and rejects the rest — computation broken into rules simple enough for a machine to follow.
challenge.fact: Turing's 1936 paper introduced the concept of a universal machine: a theoretical device that could simulate any algorithm by reading and writing symbols on a tape.

scenes.speaker: Alan Turing
scenes.text: This time the whole board is judged at once. Deploy Itō Hirobumi, Clara Schumann and me, turn us public, then declare the Expedition: the highest public Intelligence on the board when the round ends takes the prize.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 6 · Global Competition. Deploy your Great People, Toggle Public on each, then start the Expedition and End Turn to win the round with the highest public Intelligence on the board.
challenge.fact: A Global Competition counts every public Great Person on the whole board; followers and face-down cards add nothing. It lasts one round, and the strongest player draws a reward: event cards, followers or a new Great Person.
